query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Enhancing the boronizing treatment to produce a thicker, denser boride surface layer on components will improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard boride-based components prepared with conventional boronizing parameters that yield a thinner, less uniform boride layer.
generation.intervention: Increase the boronizing treatment temperature and/or duration to form a thicker and more continuous MB-type and M2B-type boride layer on the component surfaces.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at typical hot-dip plating temperatures (around 700–800°C) for durations representative of normal industrial operations.
generation.structural_mediator: A thicker, denser boride layer that acts as an effective diffusion barrier, reducing the penetration and interaction of molten aluminum with the substrate.
generation.mechanism: The enhanced boride layer minimizes elemental interdiffusion by serving as a physical and chemical barrier. This reduces the dissolution of key substrate components into the molten aluminum, thereby lowering corrosion rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement in corrosion resistance, evidenced by a significant decrease (potentially on the order of 30–50% lower weight loss or corrosion rate) compared to components processed with standard boronizing conditions.
generation.baseline: Current industrial boronizing treatment yielding a thinner boride layer with known corrosion rates under molten-aluminum exposure.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected at the operational temperature range (700–800°C) typical of hot-dip aluminum plating. However, overly aggressive boronizing may lead to increased brittleness or spallation during thermal cycling, limiting the maximum beneficial enhancement.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the corrosion resistance improvement is uncertain until validated; there is also uncertainty whether modifications might adversely affect mechanical integrity under cyclic thermal and mechanical loads.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical boride-based components. Apply the standard boronizing treatment to one set and an enhanced boronizing treatment (increased temperature and/or duration) to the other. Expose both sets to molten aluminum under controlled conditions (700–800°C) for a fixed time period. After exposure, measure weight loss, evaluate the integrity and thickness of the boride layer via SEM and XRD, and assess any spalling or degradation.
measurements: Cross-sectional SEM imaging of the boride layer
XRD phase analysis to check for phase changes or defects
Microhardness determination of the surface layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enhanced boronized components do not display a statistically significant reduction (e.g., less than a ~10% improvement) in corrosion rate compared to the standard components, or if the thicker boride layer degrades (spalls or cracks) under test conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

Effect of Boronizing on the Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloys were treated by powder-pack boriding to improve their surface hardness and wear resistance. The variation of boriding layer thickness with time and temperature was studied. Then, the frequency factor D0 and diffusion activation energy Q of element B in HEA are calculated to be 9.15 × 10−5 m2/s and 206.93 kJ/mol, respectively. The diffusion behavior of elements in the boronizing process was investigated and shows that the boride layer forms with the metal atoms diffusing outward and the diffusion layer forms with the B atoms diffusing inward by the Pt-labeling method. In addition, the surface microhardness of CoCrFeNiMn HEA was significantly improved to 23.8 ± 1.4 Gpa, and the friction coefficient was reduced from 0.86 to 0.48~0.61.Keywords: high entropy alloy, boronizing, growth kinetics, boronizing mechanism, wear resistance
